paragraphs.heading: The land between rivers
paragraphs.text: Mesopotamia is a historical region of West Asia, set within the river system of the Tigris and the Euphrates. Its name comes from ancient Greek words for “middle” and “river”, so it means the land between rivers. Both rivers begin in the neighbouring Armenian highlands. The region roughly matches modern Iraq, and in a wider sense it also takes in parts of southwest Iran, southeast Turkey, northeast Syria and Kuwait.

paragraphs.heading: Upper and Lower Mesopotamia
paragraphs.text: The region is usually split in two. Upper Mesopotamia runs between the rivers from their sources down to Baghdad, and Lower Mesopotamia runs from Baghdad to the Persian Gulf. The climate is semi-arid: a wide desert in the north gives way in the south to some 15,000 square kilometres of marshes, lagoons, mudflats and reed banks. In the far south the two rivers join and pour into the Persian Gulf. Routes over land mostly follow the Euphrates, since the banks of the Tigris are often steep and hard going.

paragraphs.heading: Water, labour and cities
paragraphs.text: In the north, farmers could rely on rain, but in the south crops could not grow without irrigation. A high water table helped, as did melting snow from the northern Zagros Mountains and the Armenian Highlands. Irrigation only pays off if enough people can be organised to dig and maintain the canals. From the earliest times, that need helped towns grow and helped power gather in central hands.

paragraphs.heading: A cradle of civilization
paragraphs.text: The earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution took place here, starting around 10,000 BC. The region is credited with inspiring the invention of the wheel, the first planted cereal crops, cursive writing, mathematics, astronomy and agriculture. It is counted among the cradles of some of the world's earliest civilizations.

paragraphs.heading: An age of empires
paragraphs.text: From the start of recorded history, around 3100 BC, the Sumerians and the Akkadians, peoples who came from different areas, held the region, and they kept it until Babylon fell in 539 BC. Around 2350 BC Sargon of Akkad began an age of empires, and for the next 2,000 years one kingdom or empire followed another. Early in the second millennium BC the land divided in two, with Assyria to the north and Babylonia to the south. The Neo-Assyrian Empire ruled much of the ancient Near East from 900 to 612 BC. Then the Babylonians took over for a century, the last independent Mesopotamian power until modern times.

paragraphs.heading: Ruled from outside
paragraphs.text: In 539 BC Cyrus the Great brought Mesopotamia into the Achaemenid Empire, and Alexander the Great took it in 332 BC. After Alexander died, his successors, the Diadochi, fought over it, and the Seleucids won. By around 150 BC the Parthian Empire held it, and it became a battleground between Parthians and Romans. In 226 AD the Sassanid Persians under Ardashir I took the eastern part. The split between Rome and the Sassanids lasted until the Muslim conquests of the 7th century.

paragraphs.heading: A name for a place and a time
paragraphs.text: Over time the name came to cover all the land between the Euphrates and the Tigris, taking in parts of Syria, nearly all of Iraq and southeastern Turkey. Today scholars often use the word for a period as well as a place. It usually describes the region up to the Muslim conquests; after that, names such as Syria, Jazira and Iraq take over.
